questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an identity from a present condition in a choice between ser and estar
questions.stem: A teacher introduces herself with the sentence 'Soy profesor.' She then adds, 'Llevo veinte años en la misma escuela.' What work is the verb ser doing in the first sentence?

options.text: It names the job, which counts as part of who she is
It reports where she happens to be at that moment
options.misconception: assumes ser can carry a locative meaning like estar does

options.text: It describes how she feels about the job this morning
options.misconception: reads a classification as a passing emotional state

options.text: It records that she began teaching twenty years ago
options.misconception: takes the duration clause for the meaning of the first verb

questions.explanation: Ser names what a thing or a person is, and an occupation belongs to the stable layer of a life rather than to a passing afternoon, so a job takes ser even when the speaker is not at work that day. Estar covers condition and location, which is exactly what the second clause needs: a school is a place, and places go with estar. The rule a learner is given is that ser carries identity and estar carries condition, and the temptation is to read a job as a mood, but nothing in the first sentence says anything about how she feels.
questions.hint: Ask whether the job could change tomorrow without her changing.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain why a place noun requires estar rather than ser
questions.stem: A sign at the entrance of a building reads 'La cafetería está en la planta baja.' What does the verb in that sentence do that the other verb could not?

options.text: It places the cafeteria at a point on the map of the building
It marks the cafeteria's position as a merely temporary state
options.misconception: assumes estar's locative sense implies the place may change

options.text: It says what the cafeteria is for rather than where it stands
options.misconception: reads a locative phrase as a statement of purpose

options.text: It says the building has only this one storey to give out
options.misconception: confuses which floor a room is on with how many floors exist

questions.explanation: Location is estar's work, and putting a room inside a building is the plainest case of it; ser has no locative use with an ordinary place noun such as planta baja. The tempting reading hears estar and assumes the position is somehow provisional, so that the cafeteria might be moved tomorrow, but Spanish does not put that idea into the verb, and the sentence is a flat statement of where the room stands. Ser with this noun would answer a different question, the one about what the room is.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two verbs is ever used to say where something is.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: recognise that one noun phrase can take both verbs in a single sentence
questions.stem: Two clauses describe the same man: 'Carlos es profesor' and 'Carlos está cansado.' The first gives his work, the second gives this evening. What does the pair demonstrate?

options.text: One subject can be split between what it is and how it is found
The two verbs can always be swapped inside a spoken sentence
options.misconception: believes ser and estar are synonyms in most contexts

options.text: Spanish needs only one verb here and repeats it for effect
options.misconception: assumes a language would need two verbs for one noun phrase

options.text: Only estar may be used twice about one person in a row
options.misconception: thinks a second clause about the same person is impossible

questions.explanation: A single noun phrase can be described twice, once for the property that survives the week and once for the state that will be gone by morning, and Spanish marks that division with two different verbs instead of leaving it to context. Es profesor is a role, and it survives any single evening; está cansado is a condition that will be gone by morning. The tempting reading assumes the choice between the verbs is a matter of style, and that assumption is what produces estar profesor and ser cansado, both of which a native speaker hears as a mistake.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two statements would still be true next week.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: apply the stressed-vowel change in the e to ie group to the verb querer

yo queren, copied from the third person singular form

options.text: yo queró, with the accented ending some verbs take

options.text: yo quise, from the preterite of the same verb

yo buscá, because every past form in -car takes an accent

questions.learningObjective: state what the reflexive pronoun contributes to a verb's meaning
questions.stem: A learner meets three pairs: levantar and levantarse, dormir and dormirse, and despedir and despedirse. What does the pronoun do in the second member of each pair?

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a background situation from a completed event in a past narrative
questions.stem: A woman says, 'Cuando llegué a la fiesta, la música sonaba muy fuerte.' Why is the second verb in the imperfect rather than the preterite?

questions.topic: Ser and estar with a participle

questions.learningObjective: teach the aspectual distinction in a way a learner can apply
questions.stem: A learner has been told only that the preterite is for finished actions and the imperfect for unfinished ones, and now writes 'Veía una película que me gustaba' when the speaker meant to say he watched a film he enjoyed. A bounded event is one the speaker can step outside and look back on, and that is what the preterite gives. An unbounded one is a stretch running under other events, and that is what the imperfect gives. Telling them apart in practice means asking where the speaker was standing while the action went on, rather than asking how many hours the film ran.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: identify a tense and then re-cast the same clause in the other one
questions.stem: Stage one: say whether the form íbamos in 'Cuando pequeños íbamos a la playa cada verano' is preterite or imperfect, and give your reason. Stage two: rewrite the clause so that it reports one of those summers in the preterite.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: íbamos is imperfect, because the clause reports a habit running across a stretch of childhood rather than one event the speaker can point to, and the ending in -íamos is the imperfect of ir. Stage two: El verano de 2019 fuimos a la playa, which now reports one stretch the speaker has finished with and can place on a calendar. A preterite can only reach a single occasion at a time, so a learner who tries to keep the habitual sense in the preterite ends up with a sentence a native speaker hears as a contradiction.

questions.explanation: The two tenses divide the work between where the speaker stands and whether the action has an end the speaker can point to. The imperfect presents a situation from inside a stretch with no boundary, which is why it is the tense of a childhood habit. The preterite presents an event the speaker can step outside of and date, and that is the ceiling a learner meets when asked to move a habit into it: one preterite reaches one occasion, and never a run of them. Recognising the first tense is much easier than accepting the second task, which is why the pair is worth setting together.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker could point to one date at which this happened once.

questions.learningObjective: identify a trigger and then build a new clause under it
questions.stem: Stage one: name the trigger phrase in 'Ojalá no llueva mañana' and say what it does to the verb that follows. Stage two: write a second sentence of your own with that same trigger, in which the subject is a person and the verb is a verb of saying.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the trigger is ojalá, an expression of wish, and what it does is place the speaker outside the clause that follows, which is the condition under which Spanish reaches for the subjunctive. Stage two: Ojalá mi hermano diga la verdad, where the subject is a person, the verb says rather than rains or does, and the form is the third person of the subjunctive, with the e of the stem dropped. A learner who swaps the trigger for an assertion such as creo que has to change the verb with it, since the two moves belong together and a sentence that mixes them is one a speaker hears as wrong.

questions.explanation: The trigger decides the mood, so a new sentence built under a different trigger has to carry a different verb form, and that is the part of the rule a learner usually misses when they copy a sentence instead of building one. Ojalá is a wish, and a wish places the speaker outside its content, which is exactly the position the subjunctive marks. The second stage also tests something the first cannot: a verb of saying in the subjunctive drops the vowel of its stem, and a learner who has only practised weather verbs will leave the e in place and write digo where the language wants diga.
questions.hint: Ask what has to change in the verb if the new sentence keeps the same trigger.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: repair an agreement error and then state the rule behind it
questions.stem: Stage one: rewrite 'Las vacaciones es un buen momento para descansar' so that no native speaker would change a word. Stage two: state the rule your rewrite depends on in a single sentence.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Las vacaciones son un buen momento para descansar, because the subject of the sentence is plural and the verb standing beside it has to be plural too. Stage two: a verb takes its number and its person from the subject it stands beside, and nothing else in the sentence gets a vote. A learner who repairs the visible half of this and leaves the rest will still write agreement errors, because agreement is not a matter of emphasis or of taste; the ending of son is fixed by the noun in front of it, exactly as the ending of an adjective is fixed by its own noun.

questions.explanation: The repair is easy to see and the rule behind it is the part worth stating, because the same principle covers verbs, adjectives and articles at once. Agreement in Spanish is never a choice between two equally available forms; the number and the person of the surrounding noun settle the form, and a speaker who has the rule in hand can apply it to any new sentence instead of recalling a pattern. The temptation is to memorise whole sentences, which works until a noun in a familiar frame turns up in the plural, and then the memory gives out and the verb stays behind.
questions.hint: Ask what would change if the subject noun were made singular instead.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: teach the parts of a gustar-type clause and the order they take
questions.stem: A learner writes 'Me gusta las naranjas' and is told only that the verb looks wrong. Explain what a gustar-type sentence is built like, in an order the learner can repeat from memory.

answer.exemplar: A gustar-type sentence has three parts and a fixed order. The thing liked comes first and stands as the grammatical subject, which is what the verb agrees with, so las naranjas goes to the head of the clause and the verb becomes gustan. The person who likes comes next inside a phrase built around a preposition, so a mí me gusta, with the pronoun standing before the verb. One exception has to be held apart, because a quantified thing arrives without an article: me gustan muchas naranjas, and the verb is plural there because muchas naranjas is the subject it is agreeing with.

questions.explanation: The order follows from the agreement rather than from any preference for style. If the verb agrees with the thing liked, then the thing liked has to stand in the subject slot, and the person doing the liking is demoted to a phrase, which is why English word order has to be unlearned before the Spanish one can be put together. The article is the signal a learner should watch, because once a thing liked arrives with its article the person has to be moved out of that clause by a preposition. The tempting half-fix is to move the pronoun in front of the verb and leave the article where it was, which still leaves two objects sharing one short clause.
questions.hint: Ask which noun the verb is agreeing with, and where that noun has to sit.

questions.learningObjective: show that the frequency expression decides which tense a repeated action takes
questions.stem: A speaker sets two claims beside each other: 'Siempre íbamos a la playa' and 'Una vez fuimos a la playa.' What does that contrast show?

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a reported intention from a reported schedule
questions.stem: Two colleagues are talking about the weekend. One says 'Voy a llamar al taller' and the other answers 'Mañana llamaré al taller.' How do the two differ?

options.text: The first reports an intention and the second a scheduled certainty
